name: Spacelift
license: Proprietary (the `spacectl` CLI and Terraform provider are MIT; Intent is Apache 2.0)
summary: A hosted or self-hosted platform that runs Terraform, OpenTofu, Pulumi, CloudFormation, Kubernetes and Ansible changes from Git, with plans on pull requests, approvals and guardrails written as OPA policies, and workers you can run in your own network.
intro: Spacelift is a CI system built only for infrastructure code. Its central object is a stack: one Git repository and folder, one tool (Terraform, OpenTofu, Terragrunt, Pulumi, CloudFormation, Kubernetes manifests or Ansible) and the state and settings that go with it. A pull request starts a proposed run, which posts the plan back to the pull request; a push to the tracked branch starts a tracked run, which plans, waits for confirmation if there are changes, and then applies. A tracked run holds a lock on its stack, so two applies never overlap. Stack dependencies run related stacks in order, so a network stack applies before the cluster that needs it.

Rules are written in Rego and evaluated by Open Policy Agent at fixed points: who may log in, which Git pushes trigger runs, who must approve a run, and which planned changes are allowed. A plan policy reads the plan as JSON, so `deny` can fail any run that would create a static IAM access key, and `warn` can send it to a human. Policies attach to stacks by label. Drift detection reruns proposed runs on a schedule and can start a tracked run to put things back.

Runs execute on workers, in Docker containers. Spacelift hosts a public pool, or you run a private pool on your own machines or in Kubernetes; private workers only make outbound connections and encrypt run state with a key only you hold. The product is SaaS (including a FedRAMP-authorised version) or self-hosted, and plans are priced by users and workers rather than by managed resources. In 2026 Spacelift renamed this product Spacelift Deploy, alongside Flows (visual automations) and Intent (an AI tool that creates cloud resources from natural-language requests through Terraform providers).
strengths: One workflow for several IaC tools, including OpenTofu and Terraform side by side, so a company is not tied to one vendor’s cloud
Guardrails as code: OPA policies can block a plan, require approvals or route notifications, and they are versioned and testable like other code
Private workers run inside your network with your own IAM roles and images, and only need outbound HTTPS
Priced by users and workers, not by the number of resources under management
limits: Proprietary, and paid plans are quote-only; the free plan allows 2 users and 1 public worker
Drift detection works only on private workers, so you have to run your own worker pool to get it
Rego is another language to learn, and policy mistakes can quietly block or allow runs
Private workers on the older MQTT transport must move to HTTP long-polling before MQTT is turned off on 30 March 2027

story: Spacelift was founded in 2020 by Marcin Wyszyński, a former site reliability engineer at Google and Facebook who had been consulting for European scale-ups, and Paweł Hytry. Wyszyński had built a tool to manage infrastructure for his clients, and interest from fintech companies convinced him to turn it into a product. General-purpose CI tools ran Terraform but knew nothing about state, plans, drift or who should approve an apply; Spacelift set out to be CI that did.

In 2021 the company raised a $15 million Series B led by Insight Partners, by then supporting Terraform, Pulumi and CloudFormation, with offices in Redwood City and Warsaw. When HashiCorp moved Terraform from the MPL to the Business Source License in August 2023, Spacelift was one of the companies behind the OpenTF manifesto and put engineers on the fork, which became OpenTofu under the Linux Foundation.

A $51 million Series C led by Five Elms Capital followed in July 2025. Later that year Spacelift released Intent, an open-source tool that lets an AI assistant create cloud resources through Terraform providers under the same policy engine. In 2026 the original product was renamed Spacelift Deploy when Spacelift Flows, a visual automation builder, joined it.

choices.choice: A specialised CI for infrastructure instead of plugins for general CI
choices.why: Infrastructure runs need things a build pipeline lacks: state locking, a plan to review, confirmation before apply, drift checks and approvals tied to what will change.

choices.choice: Open Policy Agent and Rego for every decision point
choices.why: Rules about logins, triggers, approvals and plans can then be written, reviewed and tested as code instead of clicked together in a UI.

choices.choice: Workers that can run in the customer’s network
choices.why: Applying infrastructure needs powerful cloud credentials; private workers keep them, and the decrypted run state, inside the customer’s own account.
Terraform’s 2023 licence change restricted products that embed it, which threatened Spacelift’s own business and the wider tooling built on open-source Terraform.
